items.independentDerivation: Since e^(2x) takes every positive value, the range is (3/4, infinity). From 4y-3=e^(2x), x=ln(4y-3)/2, giving f^(-1)(x)=ln(4x-3)/2 with domain x>3/4.

items.independentDerivation: f'(x)=e^x+e^(-x)>0. Setting u=e^y>0 after swapping variables gives u^2-xu-1=0; only u=(x+sqrt(x^2+4))/2 is positive. Thus f^(-1)(x)=ln((x+sqrt(x^2+4))/2). At input 5 this is ln((5+sqrt(29))/2)=1.65 to two decimal places.
items.reasoningRationale: The given inverse supplies the target, but the student must recognise a quadratic in the exponential and justify the admissible root before using it.

That inverse-derivative method is not evidenced by the supplied teaching or prior components. The nonprinting alternative does not change what students see.
items.uniqueWholeDemand: The accepted 20 include intersections and inverse graphs but do not assess the universal relationship between tangent directions at intersections.
items.independentDerivation: A is false for f(x)=-x: every point on its graph is an intersection, including points off y=x. B is false for f(x)=x, whose intersections lie on y=x. C is false for f(x)=x, whose coincident tangents are parallel. A continuous injective real function is strictly monotone and its inverse has the same orientation, so their existing tangent gradients have the same weak sign; their product cannot be -1. Thus D is true. The printed reciprocal-derivative proof is mathematically valid under the stated differentiability assumptions.
items.reasoningRationale: The student must interpret a universal claim, consider both orientations and connect inverse-function behaviour to tangent signs; the options provide substantial scaffolding.
